author: BrentDesk Staff
headline: Saudi facilities management contracts are priced per square metre
deck: Pricing building operation by floor area rather than by asset condition shapes what a contract can deliver.
excerpt: Saudi facilities management contracts are predominantly priced per square metre, a basis that rewards headcount reduction rather than asset performance.
content:
The Saudi Facility Management Association's forum opens at Riyadh's convention centre on 20 September under the theme of smart facilities and smart cities. Before the smart part, the market has an older problem: how the contracts are priced.

Facilities management in the Gulf is predominantly bought on a rate per square metre. The client specifies a scope, contractors bid a rate, and the lowest compliant price wins. It is simple to compare and simple to budget, which is why it persists.

A rate per square metre prices presence rather than performance. The contractor's margin comes from delivering the specified scope at the lowest possible cost, and the largest controllable cost is labour, so the commercial logic pushes directly toward fewer people and less time per task. Extending asset life, reducing energy consumption and preventing failures sit outside that structure, because their benefit accrues to the client rather than the contractor.

The alternative bases exist and are used elsewhere. Output-based contracts specify results — availability, response times, condition standards — and leave the method to the contractor. Performance-based arrangements attach payment to measured outcomes including energy consumption. Both require the client to define what good looks like and to measure it, which is a capability many asset owners do not have and which is precisely why the simpler basis survives.

The Saudi timing makes this consequential. The Kingdom is completing an enormous volume of new building, and this publication has argued repeatedly that the largest construction opportunity may begin after handover. The contract basis chosen at handover sets the maintenance standard for the asset's first years, and the effects become visible over the period following the warranty.

Technology does not fix a pricing problem. Digital twins, sensors and analytics — the subjects the forum's stated theme covers — generate information about asset condition, but a contractor with no commercial interest in acting on that information will not act on it. The instrumentation makes performance measurable, which is the precondition for changing the contract basis, and the change has to come from the client side.

The association's own event carries a disclosure caveat. Dates, venue and theme come from its social channel; its website still advertises the 2025 edition, and no agenda, speaker list or exhibitor roster had been published with under two weeks to go.

This publication has covered the Saudi FM sector's shift toward technology and the handover wave driving demand.

Output-based and performance-based contracting are the established alternatives, and both require the client to define measurable standards and to verify them. That capability is what the sector's technology adoption makes possible: sensors, sub-metering and analytics produce the condition and consumption data against which an outcome-based contract can be written and settled.

The Saudi timing gives this weight. The Kingdom is completing a large volume of new building, and this publication has argued that the largest construction opportunity may begin after handover rather than before it.
